Original Owner Lets Go of 1969 GTX After 317,000 Miles, "Completely Intact and Unmolested" Driver
23 photos
Photo: Hemmings/tommyscalera
"Reverent racing men have long called it The Boss. This year it'll be 'Boss, Sir.' And this year, it'll command even more respect. Because of styling and improved performance. Looks are as they should be. Competition-car clean, with just enough dress-up to keep the girls happy." That confident 1969 factory showroom brochure pitch heralded not a Ford Mustang, but an upscale Detroit Mopar heavyweight: the Plymouth GTX. Exactly like this one-owner survivor.
Introduced for 1967 as a Belvedere trim and built as a standalone model line from 1968 through 1971 before becoming a Road Runner option package until 1974, the GTX served as Plymouth's signature gentleman's muscle car. Riding on Chrysler's intermediate B-body platform, it blended big-inch (biggest, in fact) authority with upscale exterior trim, bucket-seat cabin comfort, and understated visual aggression.
The GTX offered discerning buyers a refined alternative to stripped-down street brawlers (like the Road Runner) without sacrificing genuine quarter-mile credibility. Unlike lesser intermediates, the GTX skipped small-block engines and basic big-block power entirely.
Its standard configuration paired Chrysler's 440-cubic-inch, 7.2-liter Super Commando V8, rated at 375 horsepower and 480 lb-ft of torque via a four-barrel carburetor, with the heavy-duty 727 TorqueFlite 3-speed automatic transmission. Buyers chasing maximum track supremacy could specify a floor-shifted 4-speed manual, the $119 440 Six-Barrel rated at 390 horsepower, or the $700 426 Street Hemi producing 425 horsepower.
Photo: Hemmings/tommyscalera Across its five-year run from 1967 to 1971, Plymouth built 44,178 GTX units for the United States domestic market, including 15,602 examples during 1969. That model year divided into 14,902 two-door hardtop coupes and 700 convertibles. Among those hardtops, 13,866 carried the standard 440 V8. Because 4,004 buyers chose the optional 4-speed manual, exactly 9,862 left the assembly line as 440-powered automatic coupes matching this particular survivor's specification.
Acquiring a brand-new 1969 Plymouth GTX hardtop required a base sticker price of $3,416 before options, positioning it $219 below the $3,635 convertible and well above the budget-oriented Road Runner. Nearly six decades later, an extraordinarily honest, one-owner California hardtop, originally assembled at Chrysler's Los Angeles facility, emerges from Simi Valley, California, preserving its numbers-matching big-block drivetrain and unmolested factory character intact.
The muscle car wears its original blue finish weathered into authentic California patina rather than fresh show paint. Its muscular, slab-sided B-body sheet metal remains completely intact and straight apart from minor, easily repaired fender dents. Factory glass survives clear and uncracked with functional roll-up windows, while the car rests on clean-looking tires that have aged past their safe service dates.
Photo: Hemmings/tommyscalera Inside the cabin, matching blue upholstery outfits the factory front bucket seats and center console in serviceable, driver-grade condition. All gauges and electrical accessories operate properly aside from the non-working air conditioning. However, decades of sun and regular use have left the headliner, carpet, and dash pad worn. There are, however, replacement components readily available.
Under the hood, the numbers-matching 440 Super Commando V8 resides in a stock, unmolested compartment alongside intact factory air-conditioning hardware. The chassis has accumulated a staggering 317,000 miles over its single-owner lifespan. The good news is the rebuilt 440 V8 and 727 TorqueFlite automatic have logged just 32,000 miles since their overhaul. The “Posi” rear axle is fitted with aggressive 4.11 gears (it’s Sure Grip, of course; Positive Traction, or Posi, was a GM nomenclature).
Recent mechanical attention ensures the big-block coupe remains road-ready for immediate cruising, or for gradual refurbishment. Freshly installed components include a new gas tank, fuel pump and sender unit, water pump, master cylinder, battery, and a newly rebuilt four-barrel carburetor.
Photo: Hemmings/tommyscalera Aside from fresh tires and servicing the intact air-conditioning system, the primary mechanical item awaiting attention is a replacement heater core, an inexpensive part priced around $58 from aftermarket suppliers.
Crucially for any vintage Mopar collector, lifelong dry-climate residency has spared the unibody structure from destructive corrosion. There is zero cancer or rust-through across the floorboards, fenders, or trunk pan, giving its next caretaker a remarkably solid foundation.
Whether preserved as a patina-clad weekend driver or stripped down for a concours-level restoration, an intact, one-owner, numbers-matching B-body coupe eliminates the structural guesswork that plagues heavily modified clones.
Photo: Hemmings/tommyscalera In the 2026 collector market, this survivor's pricing stacks up favorably against established valuation benchmarks for comparable cars - a $51,700 overall model median and a $99,000 median across 2026 auction sales skewed by restored and Hemi builds. Hagerty Marketplace 2026 transactions for 1969 GTX 440 automatic coupes sit at $38,739 and $56,000, and Classic.com tracks a $53,064 second-generation benchmark, placing this example comfortably below generational averages.
Offered as-is by a seller in Simi Valley, California, this one-owner 1969 Plymouth GTX 440 Super Commando hardtop is currently asking $44,750. Combining original Los Angeles assembly provenance, a freshly rebuilt numbers-matching big-block drivetrain, rust-free California sheet metal, and honest survivor aesthetics. If all the seller states about it in the Hemmings listing is correct, this unmolested golden-era Detroit muscle icon is a very accessible driver-level classic.
